newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. prepares to evacuate Kurd workers from Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. prepares to evacuate Kurd workers from Iraq.

text.p: Hundreds of Kurds affiliated with the U.S. military and aid groups awaited evacuation from Iraq on Friday, as Washington prepared to give up the last vestiges of influence in the rebel north of the country.

"If they have in fact advised everyone to leave, believe me, America will lose a lot of interest and control in northern Iraq," an official from the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) told Reuters. "Their influence will be damaged here."

The KDP swept through northern Iraq to oust a rival faction and take control of the region after capturing the Kurdish capital of Arbil on August 31 with the help of President Saddam Hussein's forces.
The United States launched cruise missile attacks against Iraqi targets in the south in retaliation for Saddam's involvement. In the north, it has so far done nothing.

In the town of Zakho near the Turkish border around 100 Kurds who had worked for aid groups and the U.S. military were holed up in a U.S.-controlled compound, hoping to be escorted across to the Turkish border town of Silopi.
Others were waiting in the city of Dohuk, 50 km (30 miles) to the southeast, local Kurdish officials said.
Western diplomats said 250 U.S.-sponsored Kurds and their families had left Zakho earlier in the week and were waiting at an undisclosed location between the border town and Dohuk.
Officials said at least one Kurdish organisation involved with the United States had been asked to draw up lists of people ready to leave within 24 hours.
KDP officials said the evacuation was unnecessary.
"You can see the situation here is okay. We haven't any agreement with Iraq and we are about to form a local government," said Abdul Aziz, the KDP chief for the Zakho area.

"So why at this time is the American government advising local employees to leave? We hope they will protect us and that they will return and encourage the NGOs (non-governmental organisations) to return," he said.
Another KDP official suggested that the evacuation would be more of a loss for the West than for the Kurds.
"This is the beginning of something very important. An entirely Kurdish administration with one leader," he said.

He said the administration would get its money from tolls at the border with Turkey, where a stream of Turkish trucks cross every day to buy cheap oil from northern Iraq in return for food and other goods.
Outside the U.S. compound in Zakho, Kurdish peshmerga fighters stood guard with machineguns. A red, white and blue logo signifying their U.S. sponsors had been sewn on to their uniforms.
"We are under orders to provide protection and security," said one KDP peshmerga, adding that KDP leader Massoud Barzani had told them to ensure the refugees' safety.
"When they leave we will provide protection and security to the border as well," the peshmerga said.

Turkey's ambassador to Washington, Nuzhet Kandemir, told reporters earlier that Ankara was providing aircraft to help the United States airlift 2,500 Americans, Kurds and Iraqi dissidents out of northern Iraq.

"From the very beginning we have been asked by the American administration to provide them with military planes, which we did -- C-130s...We are still providing them with any assistance that might be needed," the envoy said.
It was unclear when or how the evacuation would take place. Planes similar in size to the C-130 used an airfield outside Dohuk during the 1991 Gulf War.
The refugees were expected to stay in Silopi for up to three months, before settling in the United States.
